title: Can Wolves stage the greatest of Premier League great escapes?
content:
They couldn’t do it, could they?

Well, no. The answer is that Wolverhampton Wanderers almost certainly cannot avoid relegation.

But the very fact that people are daring to ask the question is in itself extraordinary, given that until a week ago, Rob Edwards’ side were still in with a shot of being the worst team in Premier League history.

Since then, Wolves have beaten two top-five teams — West Midlands rivals Aston Villa and defending champions Liverpool — on thrilling nights at Molineux to surge past Derby County’s record-low points tally of 11 from 2008.

In their previous two fixtures, Wolves battled back to claim a point at home against leaders Arsenal and then had the better of a game at Crystal Palace, which, due to Tolu Arokodare’s penalty miss and Ladislav Krejci’s needless red card, they somehow contrived to lose.

So suddenly, the team that was stuck on two points for three months until recording their first victory of the season against West Ham United on January 3, are an in-form, confident side.

And such is the nature of football fandom that supporters of Burnley and West Ham, the sides currently occupying the other two relegation spots, and Nottingham Forest, Tottenham and Leeds United, the clubs immediately above the drop zone, will be convincing themselves that Wolves are about to embark on a glorious end to the season and lift themselves out of trouble, condemning three of their rivals to the Championship.

Long-suffering Wolves fans will naturally be more sceptical, having seen their team win just three league matches since the end of April 2025.

They are currently intent on simply enjoying a rare moment of joy in a dismal, depressing season, and are already looking forward to Friday night’s repeat meeting with Liverpool in the FA Cup — a competition that gives them their most realistic chance of salvaging something special from a horrible campaign.

It goes without saying that statistics and history are still stacked against Wolves, who now have 16 points on the board with eight games remaining and are 12 points behind 17th-placed Nottingham Forest after Wednesday night’s games.

Due to their league game against Arsenal being brought forward because of the London side’s participation in the Carabao Cup final, every team above them has at least one more game to play, too.

History is also against them: since the Premier League was reduced from 22 to 20 teams at the start of the 1995-96 season, no side with 16 points or fewer after 30 games has managed to survive.

In fact, all seven examples have gone on to finish bottom of the table. Sheffield United’s 2020-21 side, which had 14 points with eight games remaining, were the only one of the seven to break the 20-point barrier by the end of the season.

After Wolves’ thrilling, stoppage-time win over Liverpool, Opta’s percentage probabilities calculator gave Edwards’ side a 0.3 per cent chance of finishing 17th — the first place above the relegation zone.

Opta’s famous supercomputer simulates the outcome of every league game tens of thousands of times to calculate the overall probability of every team’s final league position. As of Wednesday morning, it gave Wolves a 65.4 per cent chance of finishing 20th and a 99.7 per cent chance of finishing in the bottom three.

It does not take a mathematician to work out that they give Wolves zero chance of reaching 16th or higher.

This feels like an appropriate time to dig out the Jim Carrey meme from Dumb and Dumber: “So, you’re telling me there’s a chance?”

Well, yes, technically. And if Wolves fans want a reason to believe in the prospect of a miracle, Opta does have some good news.

The data provider uses teams’ current form and team strength to calculate the overall relative difficulty of each side’s run-in to the end of the season. It currently gives Wolves the easiest run-in of all 20 clubs.

The logic for that is clear. Tuesday’s game against Liverpool was the last time Wolves will play in the league this season against a team in the current top six.

Their next game, at seventh-placed Brentford on March 16, is on paper the toughest of their remaining games, and the subsequent seven fixtures include meetings with West Ham, Leeds, Spurs and Burnley, so at the very least Wolves will have the chance to deliver direct blows to some of their closest rivals.

Yet the odds are still stacked against them. Across the last seven completed seasons, the average points required to stay up, calculated as one point more than the total for the 18th-placed team, has been 31.9 points.

That mean is dragged down by the low totals required in 2023-24 (27), 2024-25 (26) and 2020-21 (29).

The highest was in 2021-22, when Burnley went down despite picking up 35 points.

Putting draws aside for the sake of easy mathematics, five wins from their remaining eight games would leave Wolves with 31 points and potentially give them an outside chance — but even that would be a tall order, bearing in mind their form over the past year.

Six wins would lift them to 34 and provide a better prospect of survival, while seven would mean 37 points and a good chance of completing a miracle.

Needless to say, all three scenarios are implausible. But as Leicester City showed in 2015, the implausible is never quite impossible.

Nigel Pearson’s side pulled off the remarkable feat of seven wins and a draw from their final nine games to overhaul a nine-point gap to the safety line and pull off one of the greatest escapes in Premier League history.

A year later, they won the Premier League title, but let’s take this one step at a time…

That Leicester team still holds the record for being the team with the lowest points total at the 30-game mark (22 points) to survive in a 20-team Premier League.

The fact that Wolves are six points worse off underlines the scale of the challenge.

To summarise, Wolves’ hopes of staying in the Premier League remain almost nonexistent.

But the mere fact that ‘almost’ is back in the conversation again after a fabulous week is remarkable in itself.
